title: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder
description: That position has traditionally been one of neutrality - albeit while recognising Britain's rule over the territory. "Neutral" is relative, of course,
body: That position has traditionally been one of neutrality - albeit while recognising Britain's rule over the territory. "Neutral" is relative, of course, given that President Reagan provided material support to Margaret Thatcher during the Falklands War in 1982  – an act which reinforced the long-standing alliance between London and Washington in times of conflict.For Trump, however, that mutual support – the "Special Relationship" – was eroded by Sir Keir Starmer when the UK Government chose not to join the US war on Iran."You weren't there to help me", the president retorted in an interview with GB News this week. The Falklands were "a long way away", he said. The Falkland Islanders – who voted almost unanimously to remain a British overseas territory in 2013 – would point out that distance from London to the Falklands is fractionally shorter than the distance between Washington DC and the US territory of Guam, in the western Pacific.Still, Trump's words have undoubtedly galvanised Milei. As have the opinion polls. He urgently needs a boost ahead of a presidential election next year in which one of his challengers, his estranged vice-president, Victoria Villarruel, has presented herself as a tougher defender of national sovereignty and attacked Milei's diplomatic approach on the Falklands as failing.Domestic politics can rarely be ruled out of the equation when the Falklands issue flares back up. However, Buenos Aires argues that the matter has become urgent: "A clear and urgent danger", as Milei put it.With two energy companies – the Israeli-owned Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration from the UK – due to undertake work on the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, the issue has new impetus. Argentina "cannot allow" the companies to "appropriate the oil reserves under our sea", he said. "We will not stand by with our arms folded," he added.On Saturday morning Milei's office said on X that it was launching sanctions proceedings against 45 people and companies. The announcement did not identify those targeted and it is not yet clear what impact they will have.In his speech, Javier Milei painted Argentina as a reliable and "trustworthy partner" to Washington and he enjoys Trump's support, both ideologically and personally. The two men are close allies in a vision of the Western Hemisphere which Trump calls the "Don-roe Doctrine", a play on words on the 19th Century 'Monroe Doctrine' which exerted American domination over the continent. In essence, the two presidents want to see only like-minded leaders in power in the Americas.Within such a new partnership and a reordering of the spheres of influence, it's more than conceivable that Trump favours the Argentine leader over the British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, even if the issues at play transcend personality and party politics.Perhaps the key question for the coming months, then, is whether the strength of the so-called "Don-roe Doctrine" outweighs the lasting history of the "Special Relationship".

title: US hits three Iranian oil tankers after saying its warships were targeted
description: The US military says it has hit three Iran-linked oil tankers after Iran launched ballistic missiles towards two American Navy warships in the region.
body: The US military says it has hit three Iran-linked oil tankers after Iran launched ballistic missiles towards two American Navy warships in the region.US Central Command (Centcom) said on Saturday it had "permanently disabled" a tanker near Kharg Island and another near Jask in the Gulf of Oman, and "completely destroyed" a third in the Gulf of Oman."It's simple: if Iran shoots at US ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers," Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote on social media. Iranian state media confirmed that US forces struck three of its oil tankers, including one near Kharg Island.Kharg Island is a small rocky outcrop just 15 nautical miles (24km) off the coast of Iran. Ninety percent of Iran's crude oil comes through a terminal on the island - transported through pipes from the mainland.Iranian state media outlet IRIB reported that there were no casualties in the attack on the tanker near Kharg Island, and that footage indicates the vessel's cooling system put out the fire within an hour. The crews aboard the two attacked tankers in the Gulf of Oman were taken to shore in lifeboats, IRIB reported. One of those tankers was empty and the other was carrying a load of oil, it added. Tehran did not immediately acknowledge Iranian attacks on US ships.Centcom said it "successfully evaded" multiple attacks from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeting a US aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer. No American troops were harmed, it said.Admiral Brad Cooper, Centcom's commander, said in a statement on Saturday: "Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost - taking out three of yours.""We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet."Centcom, which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, claimed that the three Iranian oil tankers were "part of a multi-billion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies".The strikes come nearly a week after renewed attacks between the US and Iran, which followed a period of relative calm between the warring sides.The US resumed attacks on Sunday, when it said it had struck two rocket launchers to prevent them being used to lay naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

title: South Africa 29-24 New Zealand - Boks take 2-1 series lead
description: Greatest Rivalry Series - third TestSouth Africa (12) 29Tries: Arendse, penalty try, Kriel, Marx Cons: Mngomezulu 2 Pens: MngomezuluNew Zealand (12) 2
body: Greatest Rivalry Series - third TestSouth Africa (12) 29Tries: Arendse, penalty try, Kriel, Marx Cons: Mngomezulu 2 Pens: MngomezuluNew Zealand (12) 24Tries: Savea 2, Jordan, Taukei'aho Cons: Love, McKenzieSouth Africa eventually overpowered a spirited New Zealand, who could only outrun their hosts' set-piece power for so long, as the world champions came on strong in the final quarter in Soweto to take a 2-1 lead in a high-quality 'Greatest Rivalry' series.The two sides traded two tries each in a tight first half, with New Zealand's composure and ambition with ball in hand stretching South Africa's onrushing defence.The All Blacks sniffed a famous victory when Will Jordan chased after his own kick ahead and crossed for a 17-12 lead in the 55th minute.But, shortly after, Jesse Kriel barged through Leroy Carter to cross at the other end and, reprieved, South Africa took full advantage.Malcolm Marx plunged over at the back of juggernaut maul and a Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu penalty gave South Africa a cushion that Samisoni Taukei'aho's final-play try could dent, but not fully deflate.The two teams will meet in a fourth and final Test in the American city of Baltimore next weekend, with New Zealand, who won the opening match, looking to snatch a draw in the series.Savea-less All Blacks run out of steam in final quarterWith Springbok captain Siya Kolisi calling on his team to honour those who died in nearby Soweto during the fight against apartheid, and national pride stung by New Zealand coach Dave Rennie's criticism of their scrum technique, Soccer City was braced for a fast start by the hosts.New Zealand's smarts initially defused the fire and fury inside the cauldron, however.After a brave Peter Lakai turnover had halted South Africa momentum, Will Jordan streaked clear to switch play to the other 22.South Africa fly-half Feinberg-Mngomezulu was shown yellow for knocking down Ardie Savea's offload and, from the resulting penalty, the All Blacks rolled round the back of a short-range line-out, clearing room for Savea to sweep through some under-staffed fringe defence and score.With Cheslin Kolbe, with a perfect goal-kicking record so far in the series, having departed with a head knock, South Africa had taken a dent to their confidence, as well as the scoreboard.New Zealand had ducked and dived to minimise the effect of South Africa's set-piece supremacy.Fast strikes from hooker Asafo Aumua had got the ball away from a fast-retreating scrum, while trick plays and the addition of Lakai as a jumping option kept South Africa from competing successfully at the line-out.South Africa built momentum regardless though and All Black discipline frayed as Damian de Allende shrugged off Carter and fed Kurt-Lee Arendse to score in the 21st minute after a string of penalty offences from the away side.New Zealand pulled back 12-5 ahead soon after with the agility and speed of second rows Sam Darry and Tupou Vaa'i buying territory and Savea on hand to scoop up and scoot over following Arendse's tackle on Carter out wide.It is impossible to keep the South Africa's coshing scrum power out of the game, however.Rennie had accused South Africa's front row of 'walking around' their opposite numbers in their second Test win in Cape Town last weekend. Marx, Wilco Louw and Ox Nche duly took route one, ploughing through the All Blacks front row to force a penalty try and ensure parity at half-time.While another Test awaits in the United States, the sense of an unofficial series being on the line was tangible.New Zealand have won on South African soil only once before, when the Incomparables of 1996 returned with a 2-1 victory.Fly-half Ruben Love missed a long-range shot at goal after the interval with the stakes suffocatingly high.Jordan's try, from Carter's pop off the floor, briefly opened up scoreboard space on 55 minutes, but South Africa edged ahead for the first time two minutes later as Kriel shrugged off a soft tackle and scampered in.The hosts took a 19-17 advantage into the final quarter and, with the All Blacks lacking Savea's leadership after their captain was forced off with a shoulder injury in the first half, the Boks landed a knockout blow in familiar fashion.Scrum pressure forced New Zealand replacement Fletcher Newell to his knees, the Springboks punted the resulting penalty into the 22m and a monster maul rumbled infield and forward with Marx crashing over.Feinberg-Mngomezulu added the extras for a 26-17 lead and slotted a 70th-minute penalty to push the lead out to 12 points.The 85,976-strong crowd went through their celebratory songbook, dusting off their Cranberries-inspired ode to head coach Rassie Erasmus.Taukei'aho's try was too little, too late to change the tune of the contest, but the rest of the rugby world will take heart from how hard his side have pushed the Springboks in all three of their meetings.South Africa: Kolbe; Arendse, Kriel, De Allende, Hooker; Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Reinach; Nche, Marx, Louw, Etzebeth, Nortje, Kolisi, PS du Toit, WieseReplacements: Fourie, Steenekamp, T du Toit, De Jager, Esterhuizen, Hanekom, Van den Berg, LibbokNew Zealand: McKenzie; Jordan, Tupaea, J Barrett, Carter; Love, Roigard; Bower, Aumua, Lomax, Vaa'I, Darry, Lakai, Jacobson, SaveaReplacements: Taukei'aho, Numia, Newell, Holland, Sititi, Preston, Lienert-Brown, Moorby

title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' in foreign donor talks
description: Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what ap
body: Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what appears to have been a scheme to funnel foreign money to Reform UK.His former chief of staff Dan Jukes and ex-head of policy James Orr have both been removed from their jobs after an investigation recorded them talking about how to get money to the party from an American donor and asking a fake company to pay for polling.Jukes has denied doing anything wrong. Orr has told Sky News he will co-operate fully with Reform's internal investigation.In an interview with the BBC, the Reform leader said he was not listening to the discussion and revealed his family are "begging" him to leave his job amid increasing pressure.In a film by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 News, Farage and Jukes were present during a conversation in which it is suggested the US donor gives £500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son.Under electoral law, donors to UK political parties must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK, so cannot give money from abroad through a British resident.The proposed donation was never made as it was part of an undercover sting, but that it was seemingly entertained has sparked questions.When asked about the exchange by reporters at Reform's party conference on Friday, Farage said he was questioning whether the arrangement was above board. In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he has now said: "I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton by-election. I turn up. I frankly wasn't even listening.""I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore," he said of the conversation in the Channel 4 film."The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have came from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody."Frankly, the two individuals involved here have never been involved in fundraising before and they shouldn't have been involved directly in fundraising. They should have done basic checks and nobody, nobody should be brought to me, unless they've been vetted from."The row over the Channel 4 film has threatened to capsize Reform's conference, with Labour and the Liberal Democrats calling on the Metropolitan Police to investigate the claims. The force is assessing whether or not to investigate. Jukes and Orr - both senior figures in Farage's inner circle - have stood down pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation, but political opponents are demanding that Farage is investigated and takes accountability.Farage categorically denied that Reform had ever taken money from a foreign entity by channelling it through a UK donor.But as pressure ramps up on Farage in the latest crisis to rock Reform, he also told the BBC that "for the first time", he does not have his family's support to be in politics. "They would rather I packed it up and walked away," he said. He added he had not considered standing down, but "when you've got your family begging you to, it's not easy". Farage also condemned the hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters who descended on the Port of Dover on Saturday morning, causing major travel disruption.Farage said he "deplored" anyone wearing masks or balaclavas at public demonstrations. He added: "You should not be allowed to be masked up, balaclava-ed up and go out and protest on the streets of our country. It is wrong at every level. So I deplore what is happening in Dover today."There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days". They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats. They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029. They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest. Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage. But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.   What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake. One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions". No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty". And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up – sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage". Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said. But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera – Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say." But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing. Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling – to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

schema.headline: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' in foreign donor talks

title: The Grand Tour's new presenters: 'I hope we prove the critics wrong'
description: For more than two decades, Top Gear and The Grand Tour were defined as much by the three men presenting them as by the cars they drove.Jeremy Clarkson
body: For more than two decades, Top Gear and The Grand Tour were defined as much by the three men presenting them as by the cars they drove.Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May built one of television's most recognisable partnerships, meaning anyone taking over The Grand Tour was always going to face a daunting task.Now YouTubers James Engelsman and Thomas Holland and, perhaps most unexpectedly, train enthusiast-turned-internet star Francis Bourgeois are stepping into their shoes for the new series.And, with initial reviews generally mixed, they knew they had some convincing to do."They literally changed the car world," Holland says of the previous trio.He understands why some fans have questions about whether the show should continue with anyone else."They're completely justified to feel that, because they did the same thing that we did - which is grow up watching Clarkson, Hammond and May."The show was a very important part of our lives as car enthusiasts."Engelsman says they themselves initially had many of the same doubts that viewers will have."We've had all the same reactions that the audience has had to every part of this process like, 'Who would do that? What an idiot.'"We've been through it all and we're just lucky enough to have come out the other side and realised, 'OK, this is actually all stuff that could work.'""Now we've filmed it, I'm just excited to show the world," Bourgeois says. "We've done our absolute best and the critics will be critics and I hope that we will prove them wrong."Holland adds that he hopes people will give the show a chance before judging."Have a watch and if you don't like it, you're well within your rights, I can't force anyone to like anything."For a show built around the chemistry of its three former presenters, finding a replacement trio with such chemistry was always going to be as important as finding people who knew about cars.Engelsman and Holland are an already established double act as the presenters of Throttle House, a motoring YouTube channel with more than three million subscribers.The bigger unknown was who would become their third presenter.That search eventually led the show's producers to Francis Bourgeois, a social media star better known for standing on railway platforms than behind the wheel of a supercar.Engelsman says he and Holland had done chemistry testing with a number of people, but Bourgeois immediately felt different."As soon as Francis showed up, we were like: 'That guy'," Holland says.Bourgeois remembers their first meeting taking place on a leather sofa in a hotel outside Basingstoke, where they mostly talked about what cars they owned.By the time filming began, Holland says there was no need to consciously work out how to make the three-person dynamic function as "it just worked and clicked immediately".While the chemistry came quickly, actually finding out they had the job was much less straightforward. Engelsman says there was "no immediate moment" when they were formally told they had been chosen."It was the most gradual thing," he says.He and Holland initially thought they were simply part of a wider audition process, but then found themselves repeatedly being invited into writers' rooms and asked for their views on ideas for the show.For Bourgeois, that uncertainty may have been helpful as he admits he'd "just fall apart and start crying" if he'd found out about the job.There is a clear generational shift with the new presenters, all three of whom built their profiles on social media - and critics have been mixed on how successfully that translates to The Grand Tour. The Independent's three-star review, external described the reboot as "all rather safe" and said the presenters feel "stilted".The Guardian's review, external agreed and called the trio a "decent, if slightly anonymous, presence" who seem "quite meek and pleasant, and without any obvious dynamic".But it did praise Bourgeois, with Stuart Heritage calling him "the most enthusiastic enthusiast currently working on planet Earth".The FT also awarded the show three-stars, external and said that while the big budget spectacles are enjoyable to watch, they also feel "a little muted".It added that "the real question is whether a series that has been driven by big personalities like Clarkson, May and Hammond can survive with a new team".Hammond tells BBC News he tuned in for The Grand Tour's return and said it was great to see the new team getting going."That's the most important thing for them is to make their show. We made our show and we're really good at being us. They're going to be really good at being them," he says.Hammond says the audience need to "give them the chance" to show that.

schema.headline: The Grand Tour's new presenters: 'I hope we prove the critics wrong'

title: Lindsay Clancy murder trial has divided US on whether she's victim or criminal
description: Figure caption, Inside court as judge declares a mistrial in Lindsay Clancy caseByAna FaguyReporting fromreporting from court in MassachusettsBrandon
body: Figure caption, Inside court as judge declares a mistrial in Lindsay Clancy caseByAna FaguyReporting fromreporting from court in MassachusettsBrandon Drenon and Sheila FlynnUpdated 7 hours agoWarning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicideJodi Fournier spent 15 days at the courthouse - sitting, listening and waiting. It was a personal duty, she felt, to show support for Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother charged with murdering her three children.Katelyn Kazmirci, from North Carolina, convinced her mother to make a detour to the courthouse in Plymouth on their way to a family funeral, intrigued by the case she had followed on TikTok.All around them, dozens of women wearing pink rallied in support of Clancy. Not everyone felt the same and across the country, on social media and at dinner tables, Americans have been debating the case with passion.For nearly seven weeks, the trial transfixed and divided the nation on whether Clancy was a victim or a criminal who deserved to be behind bars.The 36-year-old nurse's defence team argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis when she strangled her young children and so could not be held criminally responsible. The prosecution alleged the killings were intentional and calculated.The judge declared a mistrial on Friday after jurors - who had heard the testimony of dozens of witnesses and deliberated for 40 hours - failed to come to a unanimous decision.Their inability to agree mirrored the wider discourse around the trial - one that trial attendee Maryanne Drysdale, 65, saw play out within her own family.She and her 28-year-old daughter believe Clancy needs mental health treatment, not prison, while her three adult sons, who have children of similar age to Clancy's, completely disagree."It's black and white for them, [Clancy] killed the kids and that's that," she said. "I brought these kids up - how can we think so differently about this?"Image caption, Jodi Fournier spent more than two weeks outside the courthouse to show support for ClancyFournier believes Clancy was wronged by the US health system and felt compelled, as a woman and a mother, to show up for a case that has given a spotlight to postpartum struggles."It only takes one person to change the narrative," she said. "This is a global issue. This isn't just Massachusetts-small-town. This is... women everywhere."Clancy claims she experienced hallucinations and delusions before strangling her three children - five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months old - and then jumping from a second-floor window, leaving her paralysed.The court heard testimony from more than 10 expert witnesses on Clancy's mental and postpartum health during the trial.But some of them seemed to dispute the defence's claim that postpartum psychosis  - a rare post-childbirth condition characterised by mania, depression, hallucinations, delusions and losing contact with reality - precluded Clancy from criminal liability.Jennifer Tufts, who treated Clancy during more than a dozen sessions over five months, testified that she had not shown signs of psychosis. Psychiatrist Avram Mack later testified that the American Psychiatric Association did not recognise postpartum psychosis as a diagnosis. These declarations only deepened staunch opinions for many - on both sides.Texas mother-of-four Nicole Russell, who followed the trial remotely, noted the prosecution's presentation of how much medical care and support Clancy had received - from doctors, her husband, nanny and family - calling it "way more help" than most mothers receive.Clancy's struggles were said to have begun following the birth of her youngest child. She repeatedly sought care, visiting a hospital emergency room, different medical professionals and even calling a suicide hotline.Many observers took that as evidence that Clancy had been proactive and done everything within her power to heal but had been failed by the system, prompting sympathy from some.Image caption, Melissa Merrill says she, like Clancy, suffered suicidal ideation after giving birth Melissa Merrill had been treated at the same hospital as Clancy after the birth of her son."I see myself in her, as a mum who had suicidal ideation," she told the BBC outside the Plymouth courthouse.Throughout the weeks of emotional testimony, Clancy, who uses a wheelchair, could be seen crying, holding her attorney's hand and making agonised utterances in court as sometimes harrowing details were shared. After one of the trial days, Merrill rushed to Clancy's defence attorney outside the court and gave him a pink envelope holding a message of support and hope for his client, believing Clancy was a "sad, defeated woman".But other parents, like Texas mother Russell, railed against "toxic empathy", insisting Clancy was "not a martyr or a symbol for tired mums"."Lindsay Clancy cannot be the poster child of what difficult motherhood looks like, because millions of mothers give birth to children and endure all kinds of hardship, and they do not hurt their children," Russell argued.Figure caption, The moment judge declares a mistrial in Lindsay Clancy caseThe discourse around the Clancy trial was prominent on social media, with many users being hard-pressed to find a platform where the case was not being mentioned, if not being subject to myriad conspiracy theories.Clancy's mother, sister and former husband all testified to her deteriorating mental state in the run-up to the murders, but her ex Patrick Clancy was singled out online for wild vitriol and cover-up accusations.There were claims that he was to blame for the murders, despite his wife never denying killing their children, nor that she had been the only adult at home at the time. This thrust him into the limelight, with tabloids snapping photos of him travelling and with his new wife. His lawyers issued a statement to CNN in August calling the facts "indisputable"."Patrick Clancy has suffered an unspeakable and unimaginable loss," they said. "Unfortunately, the tragedy Patrick has experienced has been compounded by patently false, defamatory and injurious public statements."Image source, The Boston Globe via Getty ImagesImage caption, Clancy supporters - many wearing pink - huddled outside the courthouseImage source, The Boston Globe via Getty ImagesImage caption, Those who believed Clancy should be held accountable for the killings also had a presence outside the court The case became a flashpoint for gender discussion, too, with opinions often divided along gender lines.Father-of-three Vincenzo Vazquez, who followed the trial from Illinois, believes gender has a lot to do with Clancy's treatment, doubting that the public would show similar sympathy if a father were on trial for the same charges."Whatever someone is dealing with, I don't think there's ever an appropriate time or an excuse or a justification to, you know, kill children of your own, or kill any children," he said. He said he felt "very sad and a little disgusted to see how many people are rallying behind her", adding: "I think people should be out there rallying for justice for the children. They're three beautiful kids that had a future in front of them."The decision to declare a mistrial after seven days of deadlocked jury deliberations has left the status of the case - and Clancy's future - unclear. A hearing at the end of the month could establish whether prosecutors will move ahead with second trial or attempt to reach a plea deal. For now, the debates elsewhere will no doubt continue.If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external.A list of UK organisations that can help is available here.

schema.headline: Lindsay Clancy murder trial has divided US on whether she's victim or criminal

title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong
description: The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate
body: The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate the oceans, as cartography Professor James Cheshire at University College London explained."He wanted a straight line to be drawn on a map to look like a straight line in reality if you followed a compass bearing," he told the BBC. "That was what it was intended to do, and that's what it does brilliantly well."To keep those angles correct on a flat map, Mercator had to stretch the grid lines wider as they moved away from the equator toward the poles.His map accommodates for the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem much smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing stretched.The distortion is a result of it being impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.More than 450 years on, Mercator's creation is still the basis for many of the maps we see in classrooms, on TV and online, including Google Maps.But critics of the Mercator map say there is a psychological effect to viewing some places as smaller than they actually are and others as larger, as we instinctively view bigger things as more important.For Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo, this has implicitly downplayed Africa's vast resources, population and investment opportunities."Maps are more than just guides for travellers - they shape how regions are perceived politically and economically," he told the BBC.

schema.headline: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

title: Retatutride: How the hunger for a new weight loss drug is feeding an industry of fakes
description: Excitement around the creation of a new drug, especially one showing early promise in clinical trials, is often celebrated by those developing it.But
body: Excitement around the creation of a new drug, especially one showing early promise in clinical trials, is often celebrated by those developing it.But new weight-loss drug retatrutide has become a headache not only for Eli Lilly, the pharmaceutical company behind it, but for regulators in the UK and around the world.The jab has not yet been approved for human use by any regulatory body.But illicit, counterfeit dupes of retatrutide are currently flooding the black market.Experts have told the BBC this is one of the first times they have seen copycat versions of an experimental drug, still in the throes of being tested, become so widely available.Vials purporting to be "reta" as it's become known, are being sold in the UK in gyms, nail and beauty salons, hairdressers, on social media and even by flower sellers on the street."The world has gone mad," pharmacist and director of 24 HR Pharmacy, Sehar Shahid says. "People are effectively injecting an illegal drug and thinking it's safe."It's become so normalised people openly talk about their dealers, where's best to get it from and post all over social media."One quick flick through my socials and I can order a batch of a drug billed as retatrutide in minutes - although I would have no proof what it's actually made of, what its effects would be and where it's come from.Keen users are posting before and after "reta" pics on their TikTok feeds, describing how it has silenced food noise, helped them shed pounds and lose inches, with some saying it's completely transformed their lives.The problem? Despite positive results in its most recent clinical trials, real retatrutide is still being tested for its safety and efficacy. Only 50% of drugs in this Phase III stage of testing in the US are eventually approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), so there is no guarantee retatrutide will ever hit the market. The high rate of failure is primarily down to drugs not working as well in large, diverse human populations as they do in smaller early tests, or because they reveal unexpected safety hazards.And the current, fake versions available may not resemble what's being developed in the safe confines of the laboratory.Eli Lilly's website carries a strong warning "no one should take anything claiming to be retatrutide outside of a Lilly-sponsored clinical trial". "Illicit retatrutide products may contain unknown ingredients, harmful contaminants and impurities. These products may also have too much or too little active ingredient, or the wrong ingredient entirely".Despite this, it seems there are plenty of people willing to take that gamble."Young fit patients are coming into hospital with nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, in some cases kidney failure," says endocrinologist, Prof Donal O'Shea.He says some personal trainers are not only supplying their clients with the drug, they are also injecting them with it."The patients have no idea how much they have been taking, or even what they've been injected with."Tom Davies says he nearly ended up in hospital after accidentally overdosing on a fake version of retatrutide. He ordered it from a Chinese supplier after friends at his gym recommended it."It was horrendous," says the 20-year-old from Brighton. "My body felt so under pressure, I was so bloated, it was like someone had dropped a 20kg weight on my stomach."For 72 hours I had really bad diarrhoea and nausea. I thought, if this continues I'm going to end up in A&E."Tom later realised he had given himself eight times the recommended dose. Depending on what is ordered, copycat retatrutide can arrive needing to be mixed with sterile, bacteriostatic water which requires various calculations.Dr Nas Khattak, a research doctor based in Chester, has been screening patients for one of Eli Lilly's Phase III clinical trials. He says those sourcing fake versions are in effect behaving as lab rats without any medical oversight."If users who buy it online become their own doctor, they're taking a huge risk," he warns.He says trial participants need to meet strict criteria before they are given the green light to start taking the real drug or a placebo."We request their GP record, we make sure that they're emotionally well. They'll have suicide, self-harm, mental health assessments - and this is all done by doctors."Then we come back and have a look at the blood tests, have a look at everything, and then we think whether they're suitable or not."Tom decided to do more research into dosing and, despite the nasty side effects he'd previously experienced, decided to give his fake version of retatrutide another go. After nine months of taking it in cycles, he says his cravings for sugar and junk food have gone.Pharmacist Shahid warns that just because a fake version of reta works for one person, does not mean it will "work for the next".The obesity drugs currently on the market - the likes of semaglutide (marketed as Ozempic and Wegovy), and tirzepatide (marketed as Mounjaro) - target just one or two hormone receptors. But, if approved, retatrutide will become the first weight loss medication in the world to act on three, giving it the nickname the "triple G".The three hormones it mimics are: GLP-1 - this slows down stomach emptying, signals fullness to the brain to reduce appetite and helps control blood sugar levelsGIP - this enhances insulin secretion and improves insulin sensitivity, and works alongside GLP-1 to help the body process nutrients and reduces hungerGlucagon - this is the hormone that's novel to retatrutide. It increases resting energy expenditure so the body burns more calories, promotes liver fat breakdown and supports weight loss.Lisa King has been taking a fake version of retatrutide since July and at one stage, while she was also going to the gym and eating healthily, she was losing 3kg (6lb) a week.It's also, she believes, helping her manage some of the symptoms of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). GLP-1s help regulate blood sugar, and some studies suggest these weight-loss drugs can help with some of the problems caused by PMOS, which can bring about extreme tiredness, kidney problems and high blood pressure."I'm not sure if it's due to reta," Lisa says, "but my sugar cravings have gone down, my periods have regulated and I've got a lot more energy."But retatrutide is still in trials. Does this bother her?"No," she says, "not at all. There are many things that have not been approved."If I start to experience any negative side effects I'll just come straight off it."Other users taking counterfeit versions of retatrutide have reported a range of issues including brain fog, nausea, diarrhoea, a loss of libido and no longer being able to feel any happiness or joy.Doctors are becoming increasingly worried about the side effects they are seeing amongst users of these counterfeit weight-loss drugs.Dr Sahira Dar, a GP and chair of the British Islamic Medical Association, says healthcare professionals should ask about black market products "without judgement", so patients feel able to "disclose what they have taken".Eli Lilly has been developing retatrutide for nearly 10 years. It is now fighting to protect its product and curb the illegal sales which are taking place across the world.It's taking action against peptide companies, influencers, compound pharmacies which manufacture the fake medication, and wellness clinics. It has reported more than 14,000 websites, advertisements and social media posts it says are illegally marketing the medication.Eli Lilly says it "continues to work with law enforcement and regulatory authorities to combat black market drugs".A spokesperson told the BBC: "Any retatrutide available online is unapproved, unverified and simply not worth the risk."The UK's Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has carried out raids and made several seizures of "products claiming to contain retatrutide" over the past year.It says there are a number of different routes these products enter the UK and it is working to "disrupt illegal importation and distribution".But the sales continue.Prof O'Shea says while we need to "shine a light on the dangers of such black market drugs", we should not "trash this family of medications"."GLP-1s are a major advance in managing obesity, a major advance in our insight into how the brain regulates cravings and appetite."That," he says, "is huge".For now, there is still a long way to go before retatrutide gets approval anywhere.Eli Lilly plans to submit its application for US FDA approval early next year. It can take up to a year to carry out a review, so retatrutide would not be legally available in the US until the end of 2027 at the earliest.In the UK, depending on the approval of the MHRA, it could be on the market by 2028.

schema.headline: Retatutride: How the hunger for a new weight loss drug is feeding an industry of fakes

title: Italian Grand Prix: Pierre Gasly beats George Russell to stunning Monza pole
description: Alpine driver Pierre Gasly took a stunning pole position at the Italian Grand Prix.The Frenchman, whose sole Formula 1 victory came at this race for R
body: Alpine driver Pierre Gasly took a stunning pole position at the Italian Grand Prix.The Frenchman, whose sole Formula 1 victory came at this race for Red Bull's junior team in 2020, beat Mercedes' George Russell by 0.060 seconds.McLaren's Oscar Piastri was third but was later given a three-place grid penalty for impeding Liam Lawson in the Red Bull.The Australian's penalty moves up the Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, who originally qualified fourth and fifth, and Red Bull's Max Verstappen.The other McLaren of Lando Norris was only ninth after a messy session for the world champion.Championship leader Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes qualified seventh but will start at the back because of a grid penalty for taking a new engine.Gasly's pole comes a day after he lost his third place from the Monaco Grand Prix because the FIA Court of Appeal reinstated a penalty he was given at the race in June.Saturday's unexpected performance makes him the first Frenchman to take pole for a grand prix since Jean Alesi for Benetton at this race in 1997.The result is a hiccup for Russell, who has a golden opportunity to make up ground on team-mate Antonelli, who has a 30-place grid penalty.Antonelli was employed for much of the session in front of Russell to give him a tow, so to be beaten by an Alpine and be only 0.12secs ahead of Piastri was a disappointment.Russell said he started his final lap too close to Verstappen, who let Antonellli by before the start of it to avoid running in clean air."Going into Parabolica, Max just slammed on the brakes and didn't want to be the lead car," Russell said. "In hindsight, it would probably have been better not trying this, but P2 is a good place to start."Alpine put a large upgrade on their car at the last race in the Netherlands, where Gasly could qualify only 11th. This result came out of nowhere.The 30-year-old said: "It was amazing. Thank you to everyone. It was an incredible qualifying. From the first lap in Q1, I felt very good in the car, trying to chip away a bit every single session."It felt like a very good lap. It has been nine years trying to chase a pole position and to take my first win here and then my first pole here is amazing."Russell, who had been a strong favourite for pole in the light of Antonelli's penalty, said: "Firstly, massive congrats to Pierre because that's an incredible performance."We were finishing a game of chess 15 minutes before qualifying and he beat me there and I thought, 'well, I will beat him in qualifying.' But here we are.  I am disappointed not to be on pole but Pierre was very fast from Q1."Having already blocked Lawson, Piastri then inadvertently compromised Norris' final run. He was leading the pack around, with Norris behind him, and locked up into the first chicane, going straight on into the run-off area and hampering his team-mate.Now without a slipstream, Norris was 0.4secs down at the first sector and bled time through the lap. "Without a slipstream, with our straight-line deficiency, it's hard to put something good together," said the Briton.Ferrari had looked set to be in the mix at the front before qualifying with their new engine that was believed to be worth about 0.1secs per lap.But the session did not go their way.Hamilton made it through into the final session by only 0.001secs as Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto just failed to displace him, and let out an expletive over the radio when he saw the narrow escape.And the red cars were just not fast enough in the final session. Leclerc was fourth on both his runs, while Hamilton, ninth on his first run, improved on his second but ended up 0.007secs behind his team-mate.Pole is an extraordinary story for Gasly, who lives in nearby Milan and spoke in Italian to the crowd in the trackside interviews afterwards.He has laboured in F1's midfield throughout his career, even when he had his big chance at the Red Bull team in 2019. He was dropped back to the junior team, then called Toro Rosso, after half a season, and has been trying to rebuild his career ever since.A move to Renault-owned Alpine in 2023 offered him a chance at a factory team, but they have struggled badly through most of his time with the team, and finished last in 2025.Executive adviser Flavio Briatore, who has caused controversy off track this weekend, persuaded Renault to curtail their F1 engine programme at the end of last year and switch to customer Mercedes power-units.The move, combined with switching off any effort on their 2025 car so as to be as well prepared as possible for this year's new rules, vaulted them towards the head of the midfield.A strong start to the season was followed by them falling backwards somewhat as others upgraded their cars.The new parts in Zandvoort did not have an especially auspicious debut, but Gasly has looked strong all weekend. Even so, not even they thought they were in a position to take a pole on merit in Monza."It exceeded all our expectations," Gasly said.

schema.headline: Italian Grand Prix: Pierre Gasly beats George Russell to stunning Monza pole

title: Richard Hammond to find a way to share Welsh mansion with bats
description: Explaining the move to Monmouthshire, Hammond said: "It's no secret that I got divorced last year, sadly, and I knew I had to move."I saw the house ad
body: Explaining the move to Monmouthshire, Hammond said: "It's no secret that I got divorced last year, sadly, and I knew I had to move."I saw the house advertised and thought, 'there must be something wrong with that' but went to have a look at it."I fell head over heels in love with the house."Hammond and ex-wife Mindy divorced following 23 years of marriage. They have two daughters.He said he had viewed the property, set within 21 acres, another five times before buying it."Every single week I've discovered another reason to be delighted that I live there," he said."I've never been happier moving in anywhere."Hammond said he plans to look after the home, as the previous owners had, but hopes to renovate some aspects."I'm very lucky in that most of what I'm having to do is just make it fit for my lifestyle rather than repair it. So it could be a long project. It's not going to be finished in a month or two."I'll do nothing to change the look of the place. Why would I? You don't buy something beautiful and then deface it," he said.The bat survey commissioned ahead of the proposed building work found "bat activity levels in the immediate vicinity of the building complex were moderate, and the surrounding habitats supported foraging and dispersal by a diverse assemblage of bat species".Other types of bats found included brown long-eared, noctule and Leisler's. Serotine were also occasionally seen within the same area.A protected species development licence would be required from Natural Resources Wales (NRW), in order to carry out the proposed barn conversion. The report said this must be done alongside "appropriate measures" to prevent harm of the bat species concerned.Without doing so, Hammond would be unable to carry out his plans to renovate the barn."The habitats on site at The Pentre support a diverse assemblage of bat species, providing essential foraging and commuting resources to local bat populations and connectivity with the wider environment, which is also of high suitability to bats," the survey said.It said "loss of or disturbance" to roosts, external in trees on the grounds, which provide shelter for bats, would result in "adverse effects" on the local populations of two common and widespread species.In Britain, all bat species and their roosts are legally protected, by law, external, meaning it is an offence to kill, injure, take or disturb a bat, or to destroy, damage, obstruct or otherwise interfere with a bat roost, breeding site or resting place.NRW said it has not received an application for a protected species development licence at this stage, but Hammond confirmed plans to go through the process.

schema.headline: Richard Hammond to find a way to share Welsh mansion with bats

title: Disruption at Port of Dover due to 'stop the boats' protest
description: Figure caption, Masked men chanting 'stop the boats' protest at Port of DoverBySimon JonesReporting fromin DoverCraig BuchanSouth East and Joshua Aske
body: Figure caption, Masked men chanting 'stop the boats' protest at Port of DoverBySimon JonesReporting fromin DoverCraig BuchanSouth East and Joshua AskewSouth EastUpdated 3 hours agoThere has been major disruption at the Port of Dover due to a large group of masked men holding a demonstration.Hundreds of protesters, dressed in black and wearing face coverings, blocked roads and were heard chanting "stop the boats".Traffic was stopped from going in and out of the port, with the government saying it condemned "the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused".Kent Police, which made no arrests, described it as a "spontaneous" protest, while Mike Tapp MP said questions need to be asked around why it appeared the police "didn't know about it".Officers moved the crowd from the port to Dover Priory railway station at about 11:30 BST and said "all involved had dispersed by 12:00".Paul King, Reform UK councillor for Dover West, said he had been told it was a "stop the boats protest".Kent Police has not yet commented on who was behind the demo.Far-right activists Tommy Robinson and Danny Thomas both posted about it on X, praising those involved.Thomas is believed to be the founder of the Patriot Platform network.Anti-hate organisation Hope Not Hate claims that Patriot Platform arranged the protest, saying the group began meeting in July and has brought together members of anti-migrant groups from around the country.Demonstrators told the BBC they did not want to talk to the media, although one said "send them back" and another said "stop the boats" when approached.Dover and Deal MP Mike Tapp said the incident, which started at about 07:00, caused "absolutely awful disruption" for residents."I am fed up with idiots coming to Dover," he said on Facebook."I bet if you asked any one of those 'protesters' they wouldn't know small boat crossing are down by 40% and we are working hard to fix the mess."I will be looking urgently on Monday to ask questions around why we didn't know about this," he added. "In this instance, it would appear that the police didn't know about it, and the resources were pretty thin on the ground, to be quite honest from what I saw."Labour leader of Dover District Council Kevin Mills told BBC Radio 4 low policing levels contributed to the disruption protestors caused. He said that the police presence improved over the day, though it was initially "pretty low".The Port of Dover said operations had returned to normal and routes in and out of the town had all reopened."We thank our customers and local community for their patience whilst the police managed the public order incident," it said.P&O said it would get passengers on to the next available sailing if they had missed their scheduled crossing, as did ferry operator DFDS.Image caption, Police directed protesters towards Dover Priory railway stationFerry passenger Remco van Schellen arrived from the Netherlands at about 08:00.He said: "When we wanted to leave the ferry terminal with the car, we couldn't go any further."There were people blocking the roads, the roundabout, just outside of the ferry terminal in Dover."There were people in black clothing, their faces masked, so we couldn't see who they were."Rafael Pittman, a tour guide from London, said the area had been "absolute chaos" in the three hours that he was there, waiting to pick up a group of tourists who had docked at Dover.He said: "Passengers didn't disembark and we couldn't enter the terminal as it was blocked by freight trucks."The hooded protesters arrived en masse, passed the trucks and headed towards the cruise terminal, followed by the police."Pittman added that, while the protesters "looked quite frightening", they were "friendly-ish" and told him that they were protesting against illegal migration.Lania Tkaczyk, from Cheshire, saw men dressed in black outside her hotel in Dover.She said she was unable to leave on time to see her two children take part in a Channel swimming relay at nearby Folkestone."It was quite intimidating seeing the men head-to-toe in black," she said."Because of the protest I've been delayed but I hope to get to Folkstone to see my children soon."Image source, Lania TkaczykImage caption, Some locals leaned out of flats and waved to the masked men as they were marched through the townDemonstrations against immigration are common in Dover, as it is the location where migrants picked up from small boats in the English Channel are brought to shore.They are typically advertised in advance, however, and Saturday's protest was on a larger scale.The Crime and Policing Act 2026 made it an offence to conceal your identity at a protest in England and Wales, but only if the area has been designated by a police officer of a rank of at least inspector.In order to designate an area, the police officer needs to believe offences are likely to take place.The section to do with concealing your identity, external came into force in June.Reform leader Nigel Farage told the BBC he "deplored" anyone wearing masks or balaclavas at public demonstrations."You should not be allowed to be masked-up, balaclavaed-up and go out and protest on the streets of our country," he said."It is wrong at every level. So I deplore what is happening in Dover today."Image source, Remco van SchellenImage caption, The protest began at about 7:00 and lasted several hoursChris Vinson, leader of the Conservative group on Dover District Council, said several hundred masked men had "loaded into rental vans and then descended on roads leading in and out of Dover."People who worked night shifts at the port were "prevented from leaving for fears for their safety," he added.Sir Roger Gale MP said the protesters had driven to and parked on a village green in his Herne Bay and Sandwich constituency overnight.He described the incident as a "clearly orchestrated demonstration".The migration issue "does need to be addressed", the MP said, but not by young men in balaclavas "seeking to terrorise the local population of east Kent".The full government statement read: "The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused."We appreciate the frustration of those who have been impacted today. Access to the port is now restored and traffic is flowing. Those travelling to the port are advised to allow for extra travel time and to follow guidance from providers."We thank policing partners and travel providers who we continue to work with to ensure the safety of passengers and the wider community."Dover is the UK's busiest international ferry and passenger port, dealing with more than nine million passengers by road and two million freight vehicles in 2025, according to the port's website.Get in touchAre you at the Port of Dover? Get in touch.

schema.headline: Disruption at Port of Dover due to 'stop the boats' protest

title: Reform UK winded by donations row as insiders call for shift in approach
description: Defections, those who leave one party and join another, have been a big part of the party's growth in the last year – not least the recruitment of for
body: Defections, those who leave one party and join another, have been a big part of the party's growth in the last year – not least the recruitment of former Conservative cabinet ministers Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman.Elections have been as well - Reform's gains in the English local elections and the devolved parliament elections in Wales and in Scotland.But so too has money. The backdrop to this conference was the swirl of questions about money even before Channel 4 News', and Verbatim Investigations', endeavours.In the hour or two before its broadcast on Thursday night, senior Reform figures, including those directly caught up in it, projected a sense of being relatively relaxed about it. Awkward, embarrassing, but survivable.Once it was broadcast, things changed. There was fury, I am told, and very quickly there was a sense of its gravity. "A few bottles of red were had, and we knew we had to act," is how one source described it to me. The conversations went on into the early hours.Firstly, there was anger that it would drown out a conference that has been months in the planning. And yes, it has dominated conversation here in Birmingham.Secondly, there was widespread concern about the image it projected, the impression it would leave.Reform wants to project itself as a prospective party of government.And yet the headlines allow critics to claim they are not just ramshackle and amateurish but can point to what looks like a pattern of activity, consciously pursued, to breach the law.Absolutely not, Nigel Farage insisted to me, there was no such pattern.But what of the ethos of the party? Journalist Tim Shipman in The Spectator writes , externalthat "it is the experience of everyone I have ever known near the summit of politics that political operations take their character and operating logic from the person at the apex of the triangle. Leaders set culture."There is something in this. Take Rishi Sunak's Downing Street operation and Boris Johnson's. They were wildly different culturally, reflecting the very different characters at their helm. Would all the things that happened during Partygate under Johnson have happened under Sunak? Unlikely, I would have thought.Some within Reform, who are full of admiration for Nigel Farage's chutzpah and gift as a communicator, are desperate to see a behind-the-scenes cultural shift that minimises the chances of further embarrassments. And, alongside that, a step up in the infrastructure and personnel to match.Farage's team express frustration that this is precisely what they have been doing, but some are telling them internally they need to move more quickly.Both James Orr, the party's head of policy; and Dan Jukes, Farage's right-hand man, will be missed profoundly by those inside the party.Privately, some wonder if Orr may yet return.Jukes, who has been a pivotal and loyal figure in Team Farage for years, was already dividing his time between the UK and the United States as his wife and baby are on the other side of the Atlantic.Perhaps, some senior figures suggest, his immediate future might be in America. Does he return when the general election is nearer? Let's see.Reform leave Birmingham winded and wounded by the last few days, their days in the sun overshadowed.The question is how they deal with this and respond to it, in the coming weeks and months.

schema.headline: Reform UK winded by donations row as insiders call for shift in approach

title: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding
description: A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before collidin
body: A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before colliding with a marked police car.Officers had been pursuing the car for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.Fuller, whose force covers an area of north-east England that includes Middlesbrough and Teesside, recalled being asleep when the duty commander rang her with the news."No matter how tragic and devastated you feel, we swing into action and we do what we need to do," she said.The home secretary announced this week that Cleveland Police would be given an extra £2m to deal with the fallout from the crash, with 200 officers drafted in from elsewhere.Fuller told the BBC on Friday that she was grateful for the support the force had been given, but added: "I need that all the time."Cleveland's Labour police and crime commissioner has previously said the force needed an extra £20m a year to hire more officers and crack down on organised crime.Cleveland Police is grappling with the highest recorded crime rate of anywhere in England and Wales, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures for the year to March show.It also ranks highest for burglary, sexual offences, violence with injury, and criminal damage and arson.Fuller said Cleveland Police had also experienced the largest decrease in the number of officers since 2010 and was staffed as if it were a rural force."It absolutely needs to change," she said. Fuller expressed hope that reform to policing across the country was on the horizon, and that Cleveland Police would become one of the "big, strategic forces that have the resource, the flex and the capability to surge when they need to surge".She added: "In the meantime, we need additional funding... to take us to that point."Recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.Fuller denied that gangs had control over parts of Middlesbrough, describing it as a "complex" area to police, with high rates of school absence, drug addiction and mental health issues."We're doing the very, very best with what we've got - and we absolutely do need more."Authorities say high deprivation and unemployment in the area are fuelling organised crime."When young people have little aspiration or hope, who don't have confidence in the state, then unfortunately criminals exploit these people," Fuller said. "They give confidence, and they give them hope, and they give them aspiration. And sadly what that means is young people doing things without thought of consequences."The five who died in the Volkswagen on 22 August were aged between 17 and 23. Four of them had previous convictions, including for assaulting police officers and theft, Cleveland Police previously said.Since the crash, the force has responded to at least two incidents it believes are in retaliation for the crash.It has also had to grapple with a house fire in Middlesbrough that killed a woman and her niece, and left several others injured, which police could not rule out was linked to organised crime.A 23-year-old man has been charged with murder in relation to the deaths of Natalie McDonald, 34, and Valentina Foster, seven.Fuller also paid tribute to the two officers who died in the A66 crash - PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough."My heart goes out to their families - it really does," she said. "My grief can't compare to theirs, nor to the officers and staff who've worked closely with Matty and Tom for a long time."The Home Office said it was grateful to Cleveland Police for delivering a robust response in difficult circumstances. A spokesperson said: "We have been in regular contact with Cleveland Police and local leaders, ensuring they have the support they need and engaging on their financial concerns."This additional £2m targeted funding will help Cleveland Police tackle serious crime. Beyond this, the force will receive up to £197.8m in funding in the 2026/2027 financial year - a 3.7% uplift in cash."We have also committed to a wider review of the police funding formula to ensure that force funding is fair and responsive to local needs."

schema.headline: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding

title: Reform promises to increase tax-free personal allowance to £15,000
description: Reform UK is promising to increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000, if it wins the next general election.Robert Jenrick, the party's econom
body: Reform UK is promising to increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000, if it wins the next general election.Robert Jenrick, the party's economic spokesman, has pledged to introduce the tax cut within the first 100 days if he became chancellor saying it would provide "money that people really need right now".It is seen by Reform insiders as the flagship policy announcement of its conference and perhaps their biggest tax policy between now and the general election.Asked about two senior Reform aides being investigated by the party following a Channel 4 News undercover broadcast into claims about funding, Jenrick told the BBC Nigel Farage had acted swiftly and they had been suspended. In undercover filming by Verbatim Investigations Farage's senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform's head of policy James Orr suggested a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations for the party, one of which would have totalled £500,000.Electoral law sets out that to be a donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.Farage said on Friday that his party had "done nothing wrong" and had taken "no illegal money. In fact no money was taken at all."Jukes denied wrongdoing and said he was stepping away from politics "in order to clear my name". Orr told Sky News he would cooperate fully with the party's internal investigation.Orr is an associate professor of Philosophy of Religion at Cambridge University's Faculty of Divinity, and responding to the Channel 4 News and Verbatim report, Cambridge University said it was "looking into these matters".Jenrick told the Today programme that the party had taken legal advice and it did not believe it had done anything wrong.Labour and the Liberal Democrats have reported the party to the Metropolitan Police.The Electoral Commission has said it is considering "all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit" and was in contact with the police.On tax measures, Reform estimates that increasing the tax-free threshold by £2,430 would save most taxpayers £500 a year and 2.9 million people would stop paying income tax altogether. It says the policy would cost £17.7bn in the first year, rising to £21bn by the fifth year and could be paid for through £80bn of public spending cuts the party plans to make. Jenrick told BBC Breakfast Reform would pay for the policy by "cutting out the waste".Reform has said its spending cuts would include a £50bn reduction in welfare spending.Half of the £353bn of welfare spending goes on the state pension, but Reform has said it will not cut this proportion.The bulk of the funding would come from reducing the cost of welfare, Jenrick said, by not paying benefits to people who are not British citizens and helping people who are off work due to their mental health back into jobs. Jenrick also said the UK would "stop paying foreign aid to rich countries", adding that "we should be looking after British people first"."Yes, we'll pay for disaster relief but the vast majority of that budget should be spent on the priorities of our own people," he said. Reform hopes to raise £10bn by scrapping net-zero programmes and Jenrick said, as the UK only amounted to 1% of the world's emissions, it was not sensible to be trying to decarbonise faster than other countries as that was "just impoverishing our own people".The party hopes to raise £8bn by reducing the number of civil servants and £7.1bn by capping the foreign aid budget.The policy was announced at Jenrick's speech on the last day of the party's conference in Birmingham."As chancellor, I will wake each morning with one purpose. To make Britain a better place to be a worker than it was the day before," he said."1.3 million were dragged into paying tax last year alone. Why? Because the tax-free allowance has been stuck at 12 and a half grand since 2021. And Labour has frozen it until 2031. "That betrayal costs a full-time worker on the minimum wage more than £750 a year. And now for the first time, the freeze means they're going to be taxing the state pension. What a disgrace."He said that if he failed to deliver the tax cut in his first Budget he would resign as chancellor."No ifs, no buts, I'll be gone."In its manifesto before the general election in 2024, Reform said it wanted to lift the threshold to £20,000. Jenrick told conference activists this remains his long-term aim.The personal allowance threshold currently stands at £12,570. Anyone earning more than £100,000 starts to lose their personal allowance. For every £2 earned above the threshold the basic allowance decreases by £1.Shortly after becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham told the Times that the "frustration" of people in his Makerfield constituency about the frozen allowance had "lodged in my mind".He later said that "all of this would be looked at" in the upcoming Budget but that any change would be "difficult given the financial circumstances".

schema.headline: Reform promises to increase tax-free personal allowance to £15,000

title: Russia-Ukraine war: US envoys meet Putin in Moscow for Ukraine talks
description: US President Donald Trump's top negotiators have met Russian President Vladimir Putin on a visit to Moscow for peace talks with senior Russian officia
body: US President Donald Trump's top negotiators have met Russian President Vladimir Putin on a visit to Moscow for peace talks with senior Russian officials.Video on Russian state media shows Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner being greeted by Putin, as efforts to end the war in Ukraine gather pace.Trump told reporters on Friday that Witkoff and Kushner were "bringing with them a proposal to end the war". So far, efforts from the US and its allies to broker a peace deal have failed. On Sunday they will travel to Kyiv for more talks.Both Russia and Ukraine have said they would halt strikes on each others' capital cities for three days while the delegation conducts its visit.Zelensky said on Saturday that he had spoken to the envoys, who have "already begun working with the Russian side today". "The plan for tomorrow's diplomatic engagements in Kyiv, involving the US team, has been approved. We are waiting for Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and are ready for a substantive conversation," he added."From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv."Russian state media reported that President Vladimir Putin had ordered a halt to strikes on Kyiv for three days due to the US visit.US news outlet Axios reported that the US envoys would separately meet both Putin and Zelensky.Kushner and Witkoff have visited Russia several times but the talks on Sunday would be the first in Ukraine.It is not clear how the US envoys will be travelling from Moscow to Kyiv.Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.Delegations from Ukraine have attended talks in the US over the past 18 months.Earlier on Saturday, Zelensky said Russia had fired "demonstrative" strikes on airports in Kyiv and Boryspil overnight ahead of his planned meeting with the US.Ukraine's president added: "Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport."Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.Zelensky said on Friday he would guarantee the safety of Russian airspace during the envoys' visit and called for Russia to do the same for Ukraine.He also said an overnight Russian strike on a civilian building in the Dnipro region killed four people and injured five others.Witkoff and Kushner's visit to Moscow comes just over a week after a rare visit to the Russian capital by the head of the CIA, John Ratcliffe. There was no official comment from Washington or the Kremlin on what was discussed. Speaking last week, Trump described the meeting as "semi-routine".Last year, the US, Ukraine and Russia separately suggested that a deal to end the war was edging closer following a flurry of talks brokered by the Americans. European allies also held talks in Paris but discussions ultimately ended without a breakthrough. Key disagreements remain between the warring sides on issues such as territory and security guarantees for Ukraine. In recent months, both Russia and Ukraine have intensified their aerial attacks as fighting continues.Ukraine said it has struggled to repel ballistic missile attacks due to a lack of interceptor missiles, while Kyiv has focused its strikes on Russian economic infrastructure targets.

schema.headline: Russia-Ukraine war: US envoys meet Putin in Moscow for Ukraine talks
